title: Feedback Loops are All You Need — Mehedi Hassan, Granola

primary.label: Observability, Reliability & LLMOps
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 60%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is a product engineer's account of shipping AI features, emphasizing UX personalization, user feedback loops, and the gap between playground demos and real user experience. Granola is a personal productivity meeting notes app with AI features for individual users. The talk covers production deployment challenges and iterative development of AI features through feedback loops. Requires basic familiarity with LLM concepts and tool calling, accessible to product engineers and builders. Conference presentation at AI Engineer with live demos and Q&A. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with character-level positions.

summary: Mehedi Hassan, a product engineer at Granola, presents an honest account of the gap between AI features that work in the playground and those that survive production. Granola is a meeting notes app that accesses system transcription and microphone audio, generates real-time transcriptions, and produces notes aligned with user-written annotations. Their philosophy is to not get in the user's way. When Granola shipped a chat feature for asking questions about meetings, one-shotting a generic chatbot led to predictable problems: slow web search, mismatched follow-up emails, and misinterpreted coaching queries. Web search, which LLM providers present as a single line of code, brings hidden complications—token costs around 10 pence per chat, context blowup on complex queries, and silent degradation when providers ship overnight updates. Hassan notes billion-dollar companies exist solely for web search, underscoring its complexity. Personalization is equally hard: a single prompt cannot serve a salesperson wanting deal summaries, an engineer wanting blockers and Linear tickets, and an HR manager with different needs. LLMs are stubborn and their behavior is a black box. Granola built custom internal tracing tools using AI SDK wrappers and a database, with a frontend UI designed for all employees—engineers, product, data, and CX—not just those with CloudWatch access. The founder personally traces agent loops front to back to diagnose failures. To accelerate iteration, Granola refactored their Electron app's frontend into a web shell by abstracting IPC APIs and React APIs to fall back to web standards, making the renderer Electron-agnostic. Every PR now generates a preview link, and Cursor automatically tests changes and uploads screenshots. This enabled parallel variant testing of features. The talk concludes the answer is not one-shotting better but building feedback loops that make AI features feel like magic rather than a black box. During Q&A, Hassan briefly addressed a question about moving from Electron to Tauri, noting they tried it but saw no significant performance gains.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Granola Demo
sections.summary: Hassan introduces himself as a product engineer at Granola, a meeting notes app with real-time transcription via system audio and microphone access. He demos Granola recording a previous talk, showing how user-written annotations (e.g., '20% overlap') influence the generated notes. The product philosophy is to not get in the user's way.

sections.title: Challenges of Shipping Generic AI Chat Features
sections.summary: Hassan shows a fake Granola app with a one-shot chat feature and lists common user complaints: web search too slow, follow-up emails not matching user style, coaching queries misinterpreted. He frames these as predictable problems with generic chatbots and asks how to get around them.

sections.title: Web Search Complications
sections.summary: Web search looks like a line of code from LLM providers but brings hidden complications: token usage and cost bubble up (~10p per chat), context blows up on complex queries, and providers can ship overnight updates that silently degrade results. Hassan notes billion-dollar companies exist for web search, underscoring its complexity.

sections.title: Prompt Personalization Challenges
sections.summary: Different roles need different outputs from the same meeting: sales wants deal focus, engineering wants action items/blockers/Linear tickets, HR wants something else. One prompt cannot serve everyone. LLMs are stubborn and their behavior is a black box that needs to be opened.

sections.title: Custom Internal Tracing Tools
sections.summary: Granola built custom tracing tools using AI SDK wrappers and a database, with a frontend UI designed for all employees—not just engineers. Full visibility into tool calls, reasoning, search trails, and cost, structured exactly as needed. The founder personally traces agent loops front to back. LLMs made it feasible to build this tooling that previously would have required a SaaS provider.

sections.title: Refactoring Electron for Web-Based Testing
sections.summary: Being a desktop app meant only one instance could run at a time, creating friction for testing variants. Granola abstracted IPC APIs to fall back to web standards and moved React APIs (routers, sessions, query layer) to web standards, making the renderer Electron-agnostic. Now every PR generates a preview link, speeding up development and enabling parallel variant testing.

sections.title: Automated Testing with Cursor
sections.summary: Because LLMs can self-verify work, Cursor automatically tests PRs and uploads screenshots. This dramatically speeds up testing. The ability to test one feature in multiple variants means the final product is validated in practice, not just in Figma.

sections.title: Conclusion and Q&A
sections.summary: Hassan concludes that the answer is not to one-shot better but to build feedback loops that feel like playing tennis with the LLM, giving conviction that shipped features connect with users. In Q&A, he addresses a question about moving from Electron to Tauri, saying they tried it but saw no significant performance gains, which is their main concern.
